Godalming.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Surrey Hills
s1loc: Godalming carries a heritage visitor draw on the River Wey south of Guildford, led by the Pepperpot, the octagonal former town hall and market house of 1814 that anchors the High Street, and by Charterhouse, the public school founded in 1611 that moved to its hilltop Godalming campus in 1872. Godalming Museum, founded in 1921 opposite the Pepperpot, traces the town from its Saxon roots through its wool and tanning past, holding work tied to Gertrude Jekyll and Sir Edwin Lutyens.

The leisure and activity layer spreads into the Surrey Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty around the town. Winkworth Arboretum, the National Trust hillside garden created by Dr Wilfred Fox from the 1930s, holds around 1,000 species of tree across slopes above two lakes, blazing with bluebells, azaleas and autumn maples, while Busbridge Lakes and the Lammas Lands water meadows give walkers green space, and boat trips run on the River Wey and Godalming Navigations from Dapdune Wharf.

Heritage and culture run on into the surrounding villages. Watts Gallery at Compton, the artists' village built around the Victorian painter George Frederic Watts and his wife Mary Seton Watts, holds the Historic Galleries, the Watts Chapel and the couple's home Limnerslease across eighteen acres of woodland. In the town, Phillips Memorial Park, laid out for the Titanic wireless operator Jack Phillips, the Wilfrid Noyce Centre and the medieval St Peter and St Paul church fill the calendar.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and inn base serving heritage and walking trade, with a guide and day-trip scene built around the Wey valley and the Surrey Hills. Godalming station on the Portsmouth Direct Line links the town to Guildford, Waterloo and the coast, and the A3 and the Wey towpath carry visitors out to Loseley Park, Hindhead and the Devil's Punch Bowl, so operators here handle seasonal walking, school and country-house trade alike.

Sandhurst.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Berkshire
s1loc: Sandhurst takes its name and its visitor draw from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, the British Army's officer training centre that has stood on the Berkshire and Surrey border since the early nineteenth century. The Old College, the Grand Entrance, the parade ground and the Royal Memorial Chapel draw crowds to the famous Sovereign's Parade, while the Sandhurst Collection in Old College and occasional open days give visitors a window onto the academy's grounds, its lakes and its grand listed buildings.

The leisure and activity layer is busy around the town. Trilakes Country Park in the heart of Sandhurst sets an animal park, renowned fishing lakes and an indoor adventure playworld together, while Horseshoe Lake Activity Centre just outside town runs kayaking, paddleboarding, sailing and windsurfing across its water. Sandhurst Memorial Park adds football pitches, tennis courts, a skate park and a balancing pond, and the Moor Green Lakes nature reserve draws birdwatchers to its pools and the Blackwater Valley.

Heritage and culture run along the Blackwater Valley and the wider borough. The Basingstoke Canal, restored as a 32-mile waterway, threads the area with towpath walks, and the medieval St Michael's parish church anchors the old village core. Nearby Camberley's Surrey Heath Museum, the Combe Royal Crescent and the wooded ridges of Edgbarrow Woods and Wildmoor Heath give visitors a green and historic round across the heaths that ring the town.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base serving academy, business and stopover trade, with chains and inns clustered along the A30 and the Meadows. Sandhurst, Crowthorne and Blackwater stations link the town toward Reading, Guildford and Waterloo, and the M3 and M4 carry visitors out to California Country Park, Legoland Windsor and the wider Thames Valley, so operators here handle parade-day crowds, business visitors and seasonal outdoor trade across the year.

Woodley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Loddon valley
s1loc: Woodley, a town just east of Reading in Berkshire, carries a visitor draw rooted in early aviation at the Museum of Berkshire Aviation, set on the historic Woodley Airfield where over 6,000 aircraft were built and tested from the 1930s. The collection of the Phillips and Powis and Miles Aircraft works includes the unique Miles Student jet trainer and the Fairey Jet Gyrodyne, recalling the airfield where Douglas Bader lost his legs in a 1931 crash, with planes from Handley Page and Fairey alongside.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Woodford Park, the town's main green space, with its leisure centre, boating lake, miniature railway run by the Woodley Miniature Railway society and sports pitches. Just east, Dinton Pastures Country Park sets 335 acres of lakes, meadows and the River Loddon together, with Black Swan Sailing Club, fishing, walking trails and the Lavells Lake nature reserve drawing families and activity operators across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the old village and the surrounding country. The parish church of St John the Evangelist, the Bulmershe estate and the Oakwood Centre host events through the year, while nearby Stanlake Park Wine Estate and the Henley Distillery add tasting and country trade. The wider Loddon valley, with its watermills and the Emm Brook, gives visitors a green and historic round close to the centre.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and hotel base serving business and Thames Valley trade, with chains clustered toward the A329(M) and Reading. Earley and Winnersh Triangle stations on lines into Reading link the town toward Paddington and the wider network, and the M4 carries day-trippers out to Legoland Windsor, the River Thames at Henley and Reading's centre, so operators here handle business visitors, museum crowds and seasonal country trade across the year.

Crowborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the High Weald
s1loc: Crowborough, the highest inland town in East Sussex within the High Weald Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, carries a visitor draw led by its setting on the edge of Ashdown Forest and its literary past. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, lived at Windlesham Manor on the eastern edge of the forest from 1907, and his bronze statue stands in the town centre, while the parish church of All Saints and the Beacon ridge anchor the historic core above the Weald.

The leisure and activity layer runs straight into Ashdown Forest, the 9.5 square miles of heathland and woodland that A. A. Milne made the setting for Winnie-the-Pooh. Poohsticks Bridge near Hartfield, the King's Standing and Camp Hill viewpoints, Nutley Windmill and the Ashdown Forest Riding Centre draw walkers, riders and families, while Crowborough Country Park, a 16-acre local nature reserve, and the 220 acres of Crowborough Common give green space close to town.

Heritage and culture trace the forest's deep past, from its origins as a Norman deer-hunting forest to its Tudor role as the centre of the Wealden iron industry, where England's first blast furnace was built in 1496. The Ashdown Forest Centre at Wych Cross tells that story, while Pooh Corner at Hartfield, the abandoned Chelwood Vachery garden and a calendar of forest walks, fairs and country events fill the year across the heath.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house, inn and country-hotel base serving walking, riding and literary trade, with a guide scene built around the forest and the Conan Doyle and Milne connections. Crowborough station on the Oxted line links the town toward East Grinstead and London Bridge, and the A26 carries day-trippers out to Tunbridge Wells, the Spa Valley Railway and the wider High Weald, so operators here handle seasonal forest and heritage crowds across the year.

Caterham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the North Downs
s1loc: Caterham sits in a dry valley on the North Downs in east Surrey, its visitor draw led by the East Surrey Museum on Stafford Road in Caterham Valley, free to visit and chronicling the area's history in photographs, artefacts and documents, and by the Caterham Barracks story. The Guards Depot, built from 1875 and opened in 1877 as the training base for the Foot Guards, has left the Grade II listed St Michael's Chapel and Officers' Mess behind in the redeveloped barracks village.

The leisure and activity layer runs across the Downs and the old barracks. Skaterham, the indoor and outdoor skate park built on the grounds of the former Guards Chapel at Caterham on the Hill, draws younger visitors, while Queens Park, the Caterham Recreation Ground and the open chalk slopes of the North Downs give walkers green space. Nearby Happy Valley and Farthing Downs, the City of London's open land above Coulsdon, add miles of downland trails close to town.

Heritage and culture trace the railway-age growth of Caterham Valley below the old hilltop village. St Mary's parish church on Church Hill, the Soper Hall, the Arc cinema and the conservation streets around the High Street fill the calendar, while the wider Tandridge district holds Godstone, the Godstone Farm family attraction and the Bourne valley, giving visitors a historic and rural round across the eastern Downs.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house and inn base serving commuter, business and day-trip trade, with chains reaching toward the M25 and Croydon. Caterham station, the terminus of the Caterham line, links the town toward Purley, East Croydon and London Bridge or Victoria, and the M25 and A22 carry visitors out to Gatwick, the Surrey Hills and the North Downs Way, so operators here handle business visitors, walkers and seasonal countryside crowds across the year.

Wellington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Blackdown Hills
s1loc: Wellington, the Somerset market town that gave the Duke of Wellington his title, carries a visitor draw crowned by the Wellington Monument, the 175-foot triangular obelisk raised on Wellington Hill above the Blackdown Hills to mark the victory at Waterloo. Cared for by the National Trust and recently restored, it stands as the tallest three-sided obelisk in the world, reached along beech-hedged paths through wildlife-rich meadow, with panoramic views across the Vale of Taunton Deane below.

The leisure and activity layer spreads into the Blackdown Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty around the town. The Grand Western Canal, the restored waterway running from Tiverton toward Wellington, gives towpath walks and boating, while Wellington Park in the centre offers gardens and play space, and the wooded slopes, bridleways and viewpoints of the Blackdowns draw walkers, riders and cyclists across the warmer season toward the meadows below the monument.

Heritage and culture run through the town's woollen past. Tonedale Mills and the neighbouring Tone Works, owned for over two centuries by the Fox family and the largest textile complex in South West England, produced Taunton serge and the khaki cloth and puttees worn by British soldiers, with the surviving buildings now part-converted around Brazier Coffee Roasters. The Wellington Museum on Fore Street, the 15th-century Church of St John the Baptist and the Wellesley Theatre, a rare unaltered 1930s single-screen cinema, anchor the calendar.

Underpinning it all is a guest-house, inn and hotel base serving country, walking and business trade, with a guide scene built around the monument and the Blackdowns. Wellington has no station of its own, so visitors arrive through Taunton on the Great Western main line and the M5 at junction 26, which carries day-trippers out to the Quantock Hills, the Brendon Hills and the Somerset coast, so operators here handle seasonal walking and heritage crowds across the year.

Bathgate.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of West Lothian
s1loc: Bathgate, a historic town in West Lothian set midway between Edinburgh and Glasgow, carries a visitor draw rooted in its mining and shale-oil past. The Bennie Museum, opened in 1989 and named after the inventor Alexander Bennie, holds an eclectic free collection of artefacts on the town's coal, railway, agricultural and domestic life, while the statue of the chemist James Young Simpson, the Bathgate-born pioneer of chloroform anaesthesia, and the old Steelyard market place anchor the historic core.

The leisure and activity layer spreads into the scenic Bathgate Hills just north of town. Cairnpapple Hill, the 4,000-year-old prehistoric burial and ceremonial site in the care of Historic Environment Scotland, gives coast-to-coast views on a clear day, while Beecraigs Country Park nearby holds walking trails, a deer park and a loch, and Xcite Bathgate in Balbardie Park of Peace runs a 25-metre swimming pool, soft play and a nine-hole golf course for visiting families.

Heritage and culture trace the town through Balbardie Park, the Victorian Bathgate Academy founded on a bequest from the merchant John Newland, and the Regal Theatre on North Bridge Street, with the wider Five Sisters Zoo and the shale bings of West Lothian close by. The Bathgate Highland Games, the Bathgate Procession and a calendar of events fill the year, while the town's mining and motor-works heritage gives visitors a strong local round.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house base serving business and Central Belt trade, with chains clustered toward the M8. Bathgate station on the reopened Edinburgh to Glasgow line via Airdrie links the town directly to both cities, and the M8 and M9 carry visitors out to Linlithgow Palace, the Falkirk Wheel and The Kelpies, so operators here handle business visitors, heritage crowds and seasonal day-trippers across the year.
